REFLECTION / DRAFT FOR THE STUDENT TO PERSONALIZE

The evidence changed the question.

A good planning tool should make it easy to see both the opportunity and the uncertainty.

The project began with the idea that a sudden visitor surge in one city could benefit neighboring communities. The selected Arizona park data did not support that starting assumption: each of the six parks recorded fewer visits in 2025 than in 2024. We therefore shifted the question toward seasonal side-trip promotion, rather than presenting a surge that the data could not establish.

The strongest evidence concerns timing. Slide Rock’s summer concentration differs from the spring pattern at Dead Horse Ranch and Jerome. This supports considering different seasonal offers, but it does not show that visitors will choose them. A person seeking swimming may have little interest in a museum, and a quieter park may have limited staffing or challenging weather.

The spending research adds an economic reason to examine regional itineraries, but the estimates cover areas within 50 miles of each park. They are not money received exclusively by the host town, and they cannot be treated as the additional revenue a marketing campaign would generate. Similarly, Sedona’s resident survey provides a reason to take local impacts seriously; it does not speak for the communities that would receive visitors.

The resulting website is a screening tool for small, measurable pilots. It can help planners explain why a destination and season deserve consideration, identify missing evidence and make the next research step concrete. It cannot establish carrying capacity, community consent, the best allocation of a marketing budget, or a causal reduction in congestion.

Before submission, add a short account of your own role: which assumptions you revised, what you checked, and what you learned from using an agent to collect and communicate evidence.
